extracted.intended_audience: readers of political memoirs, journalists, historians, and students of American political life
extracted.subtask_description: First‑person political/memoir prose recounting episodes in late‑19th century American public life, offering observations and prescriptive comments for journalists and politicians. Useful as a model or source of opinionated guidance on political conduct, appointments, and messaging.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journalist's duty to speak out
rubrics_metrics.description: "I have answered by asserting the right and duty of the journalist to talk out in meeting, flatly repudiating the claims as well as the obligations of the organ grinder they had sought to put upon me..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author asserts a normative criterion for journalists: they have both the right and duty to speak candidly (to 'talk out') rather than act as compliant 'organ grinders' for political interests. Context: defense of criticizing Democratic presidents when necessary; exemplified by the closing retort quoted in the passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stand firmly on principle in political messaging (tariff example)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Take it as your guiding star. Stand upon it. Reiterate it. Emphasize it, amplify it, but do not subtract a thought, do not erase a word."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct advice to a political leader (Cleveland) about the tariff/platform: adopt an unwavering public stance on a core policy (here revenue reform), repeat and amplify it rather than qualifying it. The passage frames this as the way to gain votes in the West even if it costs some in the East.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sectionalism; prioritize national unity
rubrics_metrics.description: "If sectionalism be not dead it should have no place in popular consideration."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative claim that old sectional (North/South) animosities ought to be discarded from public debate. The surrounding text argues that reconciliation—symbolic and practical—has progressed and that reviving sectional passions only harms the nation's future.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use symbolic acts of reconciliation to heal divisions
rubrics_metrics.description: When McKinley "signed the commissions of Joseph Wheeler and Fitzhugh Lee... he made official announcement that the War of Sections was over and gave complete amnesty to the people and the soldiers of the South."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author treats appointments and public honors to former adversaries as effective, constructive signals of national reconciliation. Such gestures (military commissions, monuments, inclusion in public honors) are presented as practical steps toward unity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against concentration of political power
rubrics_metrics.description: "The one-party power we have escaped; the one-man power we have escaped."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An evaluative principle warning that the republic should avoid domination by a single party or an individual. Linked passages discuss threats from demoralization of wealth, abuse of power, and excessive prosperity; vigilance and civic virtue are recommended safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of eccentric or personally favored appointments; vet nominees
rubrics_metrics.description: "The President had a way of sudden fancies to new and sometimes queer people. Many of his appointments were eccentric and fell like bombshells upon the Senate..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Narrative example (Keiley) shows how appointments made from personal fancy or without adequate vetting can cause diplomatic/social problems and Senate rejection. Implicit guidance: appointments should be more carefully considered and checked for suitability and acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as a political tool
rubrics_metrics.description: "Humor has played no small part in our politics."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation that satire and humor (examples: Mark Twain's characters; Senator Pomeroy as 'Old Pom') have been influential in political life, serving to expose hypocrisy and shape public opinion. The passage implies using wit and satire can be an effective political device.
